doc.title: Ruth Lion interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: 52nd Street and Alfred's high standards in the studio
summary: They heard Parker, Gillespie and Garner on 52nd Street; Alfred wrote 'not good enough for Blue Note' on masters he rejected.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Did you two have a chance to experience the 52nd Street heyday in New York?

Yes, very much so, yeah. From one club to another and it was absolutely divine. You could hear everybody: Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Erroll Garner, yeah. It was — somehow you were aware that this was tremendous, but you didn’t realize that it had its time like everything.
Yeah, but it was magnificent. You could walk in and hear — all those clubs. You could just walk in and just hear the most wonderful music.
Were there ever any really difficult recording sessions that you attended, that just either didn’t happen or somehow miraculously did come through but it didn’t look like they were?

I would say, I don’t know what the percentage is, but his standards were so high that often times he’d write on the master, the mother, he’d write, “This record not good enough for Blue Note” and he wouldn’t bring it out. Yeah. Many that didn’t make it.
